# Summary

This project treats Seattle's transit system as a network and asks what happens
when stops fail. Each stop in the King County Metro schedule feed is a node, and
two stops are tied when a vehicle serves them back to back on a trip. The network
has 6,271 stops and 7,025 ties. I describe its structure, rank stops by
betweenness centrality to find the bridges between neighborhoods, and then remove
stops in three ways (at random, by highest degree, and by highest betweenness)
while tracking the size of the largest connected piece.

Two results stand out.

1. **The biggest chokepoint is the SR 520 floating bridge corridor, not downtown
   Seattle.** The five highest-betweenness stops all sit on it, and each has only
   4 to 7 direct connections.
2. **Fragmentation does not follow the usual textbook pattern.** Removing the
   highest-degree stops broke the network fastest. After 5% of stops were
   removed, the largest connected piece fell from 99.5% to about 42% of stops.
   Betweenness-targeted removal halved the network at about 14% removed, and
   random removal at about 17%.

The network is mostly long chains of stops joined by a thin layer of junctions,
and that structure explains why it fails the way it does.

# Data and Setup

## Packages

```{r packages}
library(readr)     # reading the CSV files
library(dplyr)     # data wrangling
library(tidyr)     # reshaping data for plots
library(tibble)    # tidy tables
library(knitr)     # clean tables
library(igraph)    # network analysis
library(ggraph)    # network visualization
library(ggplot2)   # general plotting

theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 12))
```

## About the data

The data come from the King County Metro General Transit Feed Specification
(GTFS) schedule feed, published by King County Metro Transit and available at
<https://metro.kingcounty.gov/GTFS/google_transit.zip> (mirror:
<https://www.soundtransit.org/GTFS-KCM/google_transit.zip>). I downloaded it on
November 18, 2026. It is version FAL26-161.5 and covers scheduled service from
October 29, 2026 to March 26, 2027. GTFS is the standard open format transit
agencies use to publish schedules. This feed includes Metro bus service, the
Seattle Streetcar, the King County Water Taxi, Sound Transit Link light rail, and
some Sound Transit Express service (142 routes and 31,484 trips). Because GTFS is
schedule data, the network shows planned service, not ridership or real-time
operations.

I converted the feed into two tables by sorting `stop_times.txt` by trip and stop
sequence and linking each stop to the next one:

- `nodes.csv` has one row per stop: `id`, `name`, `x` and `y` (longitude and
  latitude), plus precomputed `degree` and `betweenness` used for checking.
- `edges.csv` has one row per tie: `from` and `to`, the stop ids served
  consecutively on at least one trip.

The network is one-mode, undirected, and unweighted. A tie means that a vehicle
travels directly between two stops, in either direction.

> Data credit (required by King County): *Transit scheduling, geographic, and
> real-time data provided by permission of King County.*

## Building the graph

```{r build-graph}
nodes <- read_csv("nodes.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
edges <- read_csv("edges.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

g <- graph_from_data_frame(d = edges, vertices = nodes, directed = FALSE)

g
```

The graph has 6,271 nodes and 7,025 ties. These counts use raw stop IDs. The same
physical stop is often split into several IDs by direction or bay, so I test a
merged version in the sensitivity check near the end.

# Exploring the Network

## Map of the network

The plot uses each stop's real longitude and latitude, so the network keeps the
shape of the region. Node size shows betweenness centrality (how often a stop lies
on shortest routes between other stops). Node color shows degree (the number of
direct connections). The five highest-betweenness stops are ringed in red.

```{r geo-plot, fig.width=9, fig.height=9}
V(g)$betweenness_r <- betweenness(g, directed = FALSE, normalized = TRUE)
top5 <- V(g)$name[order(-V(g)$betweenness_r, V(g)$name)][1:5]
V(g)$is_top5 <- V(g)$name %in% top5

ggraph(g, layout = "manual", x = V(g)$x, y = V(g)$y) +
  geom_edge_link(alpha = 0.25, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_node_point(aes(size = betweenness_r, colour = degree)) +
  geom_node_point(aes(filter = is_top5), shape = 21, size = 9,
                  stroke = 1.4, colour = "red", fill = NA) +
  scale_colour_viridis_c(option = "plasma", name = "Degree") +
  scale_size_continuous(name = "Betweenness", range = c(0.4, 7)) +
  labs(title = "Seattle transit: the SR 520 bridge corridor is the chokepoint",
       subtitle = "Node size = betweenness, color = degree, red rings = top 5 betweenness stops",
       caption = "King County Metro GTFS FAL26-161.5. Data provided by permission of King County.") +
  theme_graph()
```

The network is dense on the west side (Seattle itself) and thins into long
suburban chains to the east and south. The red-ringed stops all sit on the SR 520
corridor at the east end of the floating bridge, the main crossing of Lake
Washington. The largest dots are not the yellowest ones: the bridge stops have
modest degree (4 to 7) but very high betweenness. They act as brokers, not hubs.

## Degree distribution

```{r degree-dist, fig.width=8, fig.height=4.5}
tibble(degree = degree(g)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = degree)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, fill = "#4C72B0", colour = "white") +
  labs(title = "Degree distribution of Seattle transit stops",
       x = "Degree (number of direct connections)", y = "Number of stops")
```

This is not a hub-dominated, scale-free distribution. About 84% of stops have
degree exactly 2: the stop before and the stop after on a route. The average
degree is 2.24 and the maximum is 14 (South Kirkland Park & Ride). Only 382 stops
have degree 4 or more. Most of the analysis below follows from this chain-like
structure.

# Analysis

## Basic structure

```{r basic-stats}
n_components   <- components(g)$no
largest_share  <- max(components(g)$csize) / vcount(g)
clustering_avg <- transitivity(g, type = "average")
diam_lcc       <- diameter(g, directed = FALSE)
avg_path       <- mean_distance(g, directed = FALSE)

tibble(
  Measure = c("Nodes", "Ties", "Components", "Largest component share",
              "Average clustering", "Diameter (stops)", "Average shortest path (stops)"),
  Value   = c(vcount(g), ecount(g), n_components,
              round(largest_share, 4), round(clustering_avg, 4),
              diam_lcc, round(avg_path, 2))
) %>%
  kable()
```

The network is nearly one connected system: the largest component holds 99.47% of
stops. Clustering is very low (0.014) because routes are chains and rarely close
into triangles. Trips are long when counted in stops, with an average shortest
path of about 29 stops and a diameter of 93.

The four components are:

- the mainland network (6,238 stops),
- a 29-stop component of Vashon Island bus stops, reachable from the mainland only
  by ferry in real life, and
- two 2-stop Water Taxi components.

The Water Taxi split is a data artifact. The two routes share Colman Dock in
reality, but the feed gives the dock a different stop ID for each route, so the
graph cannot see the transfer. I left it in because it shows how data conventions
shape network structure.

## Betweenness: finding the bridges

```{r betweenness-table}
tibble(Stop = V(g)$name,
       Betweenness = round(V(g)$betweenness_r, 3),
       Degree = degree(g)) %>%
  arrange(desc(Betweenness)) %>%
  slice_head(n = 10) %>%
  kable()
```

One corridor dominates the top of the ranking. SR 520 & 92nd Ave NE has
betweenness of about 0.195 and degree 6, and the Evergreen Point stops sit at the
east end of the bridge. Six of the top 20 stops are on SR 520. A smaller group
sits around Renton Transit Center. No Link light rail station and no stop in the
downtown core appears in the top 20. Downtown has many parallel routes, which
probably spreads shortest paths across dozens of stops so that no single one is
critical. The fragile points are in the suburbs, where one bridge or one arterial
carries most of the traffic between areas.

The ranking also shows the broker pattern. Bellevue Transit Center - Bay 6 has
degree 2 but ranks 9th by betweenness. A degree-only analysis would call it
unimportant, while betweenness shows it is a key link between two chains.

## Resilience test: three ways to break the network

The main experiment removes stops in 1% steps up to 50% removed, using three
strategies:

- **Random** failure (mean of 10 trials), as a model of everyday disruption.
- **Degree-targeted** removal, best-connected stops first.
- **Betweenness-targeted** removal, biggest bridges first.

After each step I record the size of the largest remaining component as a
fraction of the original 6,271 stops.

```{r resilience}
set.seed(20261118)

largest_fraction <- function(graph) {
  if (vcount(graph) == 0) return(0)
  max(components(graph)$csize) / vcount(g)
}

attack_curve <- function(order_names, steps = 0:50) {
  sapply(steps, function(p) {
    k <- floor(p / 100 * vcount(g))
    if (k == 0) return(largest_fraction(g))
    largest_fraction(delete_vertices(g, order_names[seq_len(k)]))
  })
}

steps <- 0:50
deg_order <- V(g)$name[order(-degree(g), V(g)$name)]
bet_order <- V(g)$name[order(-V(g)$betweenness_r, V(g)$name)]

resilience <- tibble(
  pct_removed = steps,
  `Degree-targeted`      = attack_curve(deg_order, steps),
  `Betweenness-targeted` = attack_curve(bet_order, steps),
  Random = rowMeans(replicate(10, attack_curve(sample(V(g)$name), steps)))
)

resilience %>%
  tidyr::pivot_longer(-pct_removed, names_to = "Strategy", values_to = "Largest component") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = pct_removed, y = `Largest component`, colour = Strategy)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(title = "Resilience: largest component vs. stops removed",
       x = "Stops removed (%)", y = "Largest component (fraction of original stops)",
       caption = "King County Metro GTFS FAL26-161.5. Data provided by permission of King County.")
```

This differs from the standard textbook result. In hub-dominated networks,
degree-targeted attacks are devastating, betweenness attacks are usually
comparable, and random failure does little harm. Here:

- Degree-targeted removal fragments the network fastest. The largest component
  drops below 50% at 5% removed, with about 42% of stops still in it at that point.
- Betweenness-targeted removal halves the network at about 14% removed.
- Random removal halves it at about 17%. Even random failure does real damage,
  because with an average degree of 2.24 there is little redundancy anywhere.

A note on reproducibility: many stops share the same degree, so the exact
degree-attack curve depends on how ties are broken. The orders above break ties
by stop name, which makes this page reproducible. The ranking of the three
strategies (degree fastest, then betweenness, then random) should hold under other
tie-breaking choices, but the exact percentages can shift by a few points.

Why does the degree attack win? In a chain-like network the high-degree stops are
not a few superstar hubs. They are the whole junction layer (all 382 stops with
degree 4 or more) that ties the routes together, and removing them cuts the chains
apart everywhere at once. The top-betweenness stops, by contrast, sit in series
along a few corridors like SR 520. Once the first bridge stop is gone, its
neighbors lose most of their betweenness too, so a static betweenness attack
spends many removals on corridors that are already cut.

## A second measure: do trips survive, and at what cost?

Largest-component size shows when the network splits, but not when it stops being
usable. As a second measure I sampled 300 pairs of stops and, at each removal
step, recorded the share of pairs still connected and the average shortest path
among the pairs that remain connected.

```{r path-measure}
set.seed(20261118)
lcc <- induced_subgraph(g, names(which(components(g)$membership ==
                                       which.max(components(g)$csize))))
pair_sample <- replicate(300, sample(V(lcc)$name, 2), simplify = FALSE)

pair_stats <- function(order_names, steps = 0:50) {
  t(sapply(steps, function(p) {
    k <- floor(p / 100 * vcount(g))
    h <- if (k == 0) g else delete_vertices(g, order_names[seq_len(k)])
    d <- sapply(pair_sample, function(pr) {
      if (!all(pr %in% V(h)$name)) return(NA_real_)
      dd <- distances(h, v = pr[1], to = pr[2])[1, 1]
      ifelse(is.infinite(dd), NA_real_, dd)
    })
    c(share_connected = mean(!is.na(d)), avg_path = mean(d, na.rm = TRUE))
  }))
}

path_deg <- pair_stats(deg_order)
path_bet <- pair_stats(bet_order)

# Selected rows, printed so the numbers quoted below can be checked.
tibble(`Removed (%)` = steps,
       `Degree: pairs connected` = round(path_deg[, "share_connected"], 3),
       `Degree: avg path` = round(path_deg[, "avg_path"], 1),
       `Betweenness: pairs connected` = round(path_bet[, "share_connected"], 3),
       `Betweenness: avg path` = round(path_bet[, "avg_path"], 1)) %>%
  filter(`Removed (%)` %in% c(0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 15, 20)) %>%
  kable()
```

I did not run this measure for random removal. Two points come out of the table.

First, pair connectivity falls at least as fast as the largest component. Under the
degree attack the share of connected pairs drops from 72% at 4% removed to 26% at
5%, so it falls below half at 5%. Under the betweenness attack it falls below half
at about 10% removed, compared with 14% for the largest component. A trip fails if
either endpoint is removed or if the path between them is cut.

Second, trips get much longer before they become impossible. Under the
betweenness attack the average path among surviving pairs grows from 29 stops to about
100 stops by 7 to 9% removed (a peak of about 107 at 9%). Under the degree
attack it reaches about 98 stops at 4% removed. Removing junctions and bridges
forces long detours along the chains.

After the peak, average path length falls again. That is not a recovery. It
happens because only short local trips are still possible, so the average is taken
over a shrinking and increasingly local set of pairs. The two measures should be
read together: the largest component shows when the network splits, and path
length shows when it stops being usable.

## Sensitivity check: does merging duplicate stops change the answer?

The counts above use raw stop IDs, but agencies often split one physical stop into
several IDs by direction or bay. For example, Sr 520 & Evergreen Point Rd holds
both the #2 and #3 betweenness ranks. The usual merging key, `parent_station`, is
blank for all 6,271 stops in this feed, so I merged stops with the same name and
the same coordinates rounded to 3 decimal places.

```{r merge-check}
nodes_merged <- nodes %>%
  mutate(key = paste(name, round(x, 3), round(y, 3))) %>%
  group_by(key) %>%
  summarise(id_new = first(id), x = mean(x), y = mean(y), .groups = "drop")

id_map <- nodes %>%
  mutate(key = paste(name, round(x, 3), round(y, 3))) %>%
  left_join(nodes_merged %>% select(key, id_new), by = "key") %>%
  select(id, id_new)

edges_merged <- edges %>%
  left_join(id_map, by = c("from" = "id")) %>% rename(from_new = id_new) %>%
  left_join(id_map, by = c("to" = "id"))   %>% rename(to_new = id_new) %>%
  filter(from_new != to_new) %>%
  distinct(from = from_new, to = to_new)

g_merged <- graph_from_data_frame(edges_merged,
                                  vertices = nodes_merged %>% rename(id = id_new) %>%
                                    select(id, x, y),
                                  directed = FALSE)
c(nodes_merged = vcount(g_merged), ties_merged = ecount(g_merged),
  largest_share_merged = round(max(components(g_merged)$csize) / vcount(g_merged), 4))
```

Merging removes 881 duplicate stop IDs and gives 5,390 nodes and 6,976 ties. The
largest component still holds 99.46% of stops, and the corridor chokepoints stay
the same. The main results do not depend on the stop-ID convention. I keep the
raw-ID network as the primary analysis because it is the feed's own unit, and I
treat the merged network as a robustness check.

# Takeaways

Seattle's transit network is held together by a thin layer of modest junctions
and a few bridges, strung between long chains of ordinary stops. That structure
makes it fragile in a specific way. Random failures are survivable but not cheap,
because a chain network has little redundancy. The worst failures are
concentrated and predictable. Removing 5% of stops by degree cuts the largest
connected piece from 99.5% to about 42% of the network, and removing
high-betweenness stops makes the trips that still work far longer (about 29 stops
growing to about 107 at 9% removed).

For a transit agency, the practical lesson is that resilience planning should
protect brokers and junctions, not only the busiest stations. The stop that
matters most may have only two connections and a name nobody recognizes.

This project is also a reminder not to import textbook expectations into real
networks. The usual finding that networks are robust to random failure but fragile
to targeted attack assumes a hub-dominated degree distribution, which this network
does not have. Measuring the network's structure first is what showed that degree
removal, not betweenness removal, is the most damaging attack here.
